answer:
1. The animation shows how inflation wears down a fixed income. An illustrative retiree, Carl, starts in January 1966 with a first check that buys 10 crates of goods. His check grows only about 2% a year. Prices rise 6.38% a year, which the animation calls the fastest stretch of US history. A second character, Ruth, appears in frames 1 and 6, and her line is labeled "back above in early years."

2. Over time, the crates his check can buy shrink. In frame 5, at year 13, the crates on the right are dimming out. By year 20 (frame 6), only about 4 of the 10 crates are left. The blue price bar stays tall, which means prices keep rising faster than the check.

3. It means a payment that rises more slowly than prices loses buying power, and the loss compounds. In this historical example, Carl had less buying power than at the start on 20 of 20 anniversaries. The small chart in frame 6 appears to track Ruth's buying power, which dips below the starting line and ends well below it. The frame 6 caption says it was "back above in early years." The frames don't show how Ruth's payout differs from Carl's.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that a flat or slowly rising payout is exposed to inflation, and that the way payouts adjust matters when comparing options. That is my reading, not something the animation says. The labels "ILLUSTRATIVE" and "US only · history, not a forecast" warn against treating it as a prediction.

5. The conclusion in 4 is my own. The animation shows the buying-power loss and cautions that it is not a forecast. It never recommends an action or says which annuity option to pick.
